```{r}
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's:
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# Feng & Rutledge (2024), Experiment 2, n = 200 (Results, p. 3; Fig. 2A):
# rare minus common risk taking = 4.03 +/- 1.06 % (mean +/- SEM), p < .001 (Wilcoxon).
original_n    <- 200
original_mean <- 4.03
original_sem  <- 1.06
original_sd   <- original_sem * sqrt(original_n)   # about 15.0 percentage points
original_dz   <- original_mean / original_sd       # about 0.27
# The paper reports no CI; this one is computed from the mean and SEM.
orig_ci       <- original_mean + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, original_n - 1) * original_sem

# Risk-taking rates by sequence type, for the side-by-side figure. Not printed in the paper;
# computed from the authors' Experiment 2 data (OSF, data_csv/Exp2_data_taskdata.csv), which
# reproduce the paper's 4.03 +/- 1.06 exactly.
original_rates <- tibble(
  sequence = c("Common", "Rare"),
  mean     = c(46.53, 50.57),   # % risky choices, mean across participants
  sem      = c(1.05, 1.17),
  n        = original_n
)
# Secondary effect (perseveration): stay rate, rare minus common = -3.62 +/- 0.89 % (p. 4).
original_stay_mean <- -3.62
original_stay_sem  <- 0.89
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"
# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id, n_choice_trials = 120) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 1e5)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # Choices are coded from the key actually pressed (b/B = left, n/N = right). The Phase 1
  # (lite) experiment saved an uppercase "B" (caps lock) as a right-hand choice, so chosen
  # side, chose_risky and stay (same choice as the previous trial; trial 1 has none) are
  # recomputed from the key here. For correctly coded data (Phase 2) this changes nothing.
  # The values as saved are kept as chose_risky_recorded / stay_recorded for the sensitivity check.
  if (all(c("task", "response", "risky_side", "trial_number") %in% names(trials))) {
    recoded <- trials |>
      filter(task == "choice") |>
      mutate(trial_number = as.numeric(trial_number),
             chosen_side_key = if_else(tolower(as.character(response)) == "b", "left", "right"),
             chose_risky_key = as.numeric(chosen_side_key == risky_side)) |>
      arrange(participant_id, trial_number) |>
      group_by(participant_id) |>
      mutate(stay_key = as.numeric(chose_risky_key == lag(chose_risky_key))) |>
      ungroup() |>
      select(participant_id, trial_number, chose_risky_key, stay_key)
    trials <- trials |>
      mutate(trial_number = as.numeric(trial_number)) |>
      left_join(recoded, by = c("participant_id", "trial_number")) |>
      mutate(chose_risky_recorded = as.numeric(chose_risky), stay_recorded = as.numeric(stay),
             chose_risky = if_else(task %in% "choice", chose_risky_key, as.numeric(chose_risky)),
             stay        = if_else(task %in% "choice", stay_key, as.numeric(stay))) |>
      select(-chose_risky_key, -stay_key)
  }

  # Sessions run by the automated test robot (?fast=1, only possible on localhost) are not data.
  if ("fast_mode" %in% names(participants)) participants <- participants |> filter(!(fast_mode %in% TRUE))
  if (!"headphone_passed" %in% names(participants)) participants$headphone_passed <- NA

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed %in% TRUE)

  # Exclusion rule (preregistered): passed the headphone check (Phase 1 lite: 2 of 2 correct;
  # Phase 2: 5 or more of 6; failing ends the study) and has all choice trials
  # (n_choice_trials: 120 in Phase 1, 60 in Phase 2). Not named n_trials, because participants.csv
  # has a column called n_trials (all saved rows), which dplyr would use instead.
  n_choice <- trials |> filter(task == "choice") |> count(participant_id, name = "n_choice")
  checked <- complete |>
    left_join(n_choice, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(n_choice = coalesce(n_choice, 0L))
  keep <- checked |> filter(headphone_passed %in% TRUE, n_choice == n_choice_trials)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep,
       n_headphone_fail = sum(participants$headphone_passed %in% FALSE),
       n_missing_trials = sum(checked$headphone_passed %in% TRUE & checked$n_choice < n_choice_trials))
}

# Per-participant percentages of risky choices (and of staying with the previous choice)
# after common and rare sequences, and the rare-minus-common differences.
person_effects <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    mutate(rare = as.logical(rare), chose_risky = as.numeric(chose_risky), stay = as.numeric(stay)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(risky_rare   = 100 * mean(chose_risky[rare]),
              risky_common = 100 * mean(chose_risky[!rare]),
              stay_rare    = 100 * mean(stay[rare], na.rm = TRUE),
              stay_common  = 100 * mean(stay[!rare], na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    # Rounded so that differences that are equal in exact arithmetic (e.g. 0) are equal in
    # floating point too; otherwise the Wilcoxon test's zero and tie handling depends on rounding noise.
    mutate(risk_diff = round(risky_rare - risky_common, 8), stay_diff = round(stay_rare - stay_common, 8))
}

# The key statistic: mean rare-minus-common difference with SEM and 95% CI, d_z, and the
# two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero (the original's test). NULL with < 2 people.
effect_summary <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 2) return(NULL)
  m <- mean(x); s <- sd(x); sem <- s / sqrt(n)
  w <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(round(x, 8), mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided", exact = FALSE)),
                error = function(e) list(statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_))
  tibble(N = n, estimate = m, sem = sem,
         ci_low = m - qt(0.975, n - 1) * sem, ci_high = m + qt(0.975, n - 1) * sem,
         dz = if (s > 0) m / s else NA_real_,
         V = unname(w$statistic), p = w$p.value)
}

# Mean % risky after common and rare sequences, for the side-by-side figure.
sequence_rates <- function(pe) {
  pe |>
    pivot_longer(c(risky_common, risky_rare), names_to = "sequence", values_to = "pct") |>
    mutate(sequence = if_else(sequence == "risky_rare", "Rare", "Common")) |>
    group_by(sequence) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(pct), sem = sd(pct) / sqrt(n()), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given. Points are
# means, error bars 95% CIs, and a line joins each study's common and rare rates.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           half = qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * sem,
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  cols <- setNames(c("grey45", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.35)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = sequence, y = mean, colour = Study, group = Study)) +
    geom_line(position = dodge, linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - half, ymax = mean + half), position = dodge, width = 0.12) +
    geom_point(position = dodge, size = 3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
    labs(x = "Tone sequence before the choice", y = "Chose the risky option (%)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

# Formatting helpers shared by the tables.
fmt_p <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "" else format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2, n_choice_trials = 60)   # Phase 2 has 60 choice trials
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
key_row <- function(study, r = NULL, p_text = NULL) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (rare − common)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", d_z = "", `Wilcoxon p` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (rare − common)` = sprintf("%.2f points", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         d_z = sprintf("%.2f", r$dz),
         `Wilcoxon p` = p_text %||% fmt_p(r$p))
}
original_effect <- tibble(N = original_n, estimate = original_mean, ci_low = orig_ci[1],
                          ci_high = orig_ci[2], dz = original_dz, p = NA_real_)
p1_effect <- if (have_data) effect_summary(person_effects(phase1)$risk_diff)
p2_effect <- if (have_phase2) effect_summary(person_effects(phase2)$risk_diff)

bind_rows(
  key_row("Original (Experiment 2)", original_effect, p_text = "< .001"),
  key_row("Phase 1: replication", p1_effect),
  key_row("Phase 2: extension", p2_effect)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllr",
    caption = "Key comparison: percentage of risky choices after rare minus common tone sequences, per participant (original CI computed from its mean and SEM).")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction
I’m interested in applying mathematical modelling technique to model psychological process. Coming from mathematical finance background, the Feng & Rutledge (2024)’s research on surprising sounds influence risky decision making fit my interest and bridge the gap between psychology, behavioural finance, and mathematical modelling. This paper also highlighted how external stimuli like surprising sounds can influence one’s attitude towards risk taking, which also has been studied in professional traders (e.g. trading floor buzzer or surprising news announcement in trading floor) and casino floor.

For the specific experiment that I replicated, experiment 2, each participant can decide whether they want to choose a ‘safe’ or ‘risky’ option in every trial, with the aim of maximising their cumulative wealth. Each participant start with 500 points and the outcome of risky option is revealed after 1.3 seconds delay if chosen. In total, there were 120 trials and the participants received fixed monetary reward irrespective of their final outcome. For the stimulus, each participant is presented with 6-tone auditory sequence, with 3 different frequencies, i.e. A=1000 Hz, B=1500 Hz, and C=500 Hz. In 75% of the trials participants hear ‘common sequence’ : AAAAAA, and for the remaining 25% of the trials participants hear ‘rare sequence’: AAAAAB or AAAAAC. Experimenter alternate the location of risky choice from left to right (or right to left) of the screen for every 10 trials. To run this experiment, we recruited participants in Prolific with the following criteria: age 18+ and fluent in English, no hearing difficulty, have access to laptop, and earphone. We aimed to recruit 120 participants in total and we built the experiment in jspsych. 

There were several challenges that we anticipated in running this experiment, including limited budget to recruit participants in-time, participants attention and audio quality are hard to control, moving from Gorilla (original experiment platform) to jsPsych with firebase. 
For the **key statistical test**, we calculated the percentage difference of each participant’s risky choices in rare trial and in common trial and perform the 2-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (against 0), to be consistent with the authors.


## Methods

### Power analysis


The original effect size is 4.03 ± 1.06% (i.e. % points of risky choice for rare minus common tone sequence), d_z = 0.27 with N = 200 participants. As we can see from the power table below, we need 116 participants (Wilcoxon) for 80 % power, 155 for 90%, and 191 for 95%. The other alternative that one could use is 2.5 times the original sample size (500 participants), as published effect tend to be inflated. We choose to power the study to the original effect and aim for the minimum sample size of interest to achieve at least 80 \% power, which led us to choose N=120 participants. Budget constraint was also part of our consideration, which limit the number of participants we could recruit. 

```{r}
#| label: power
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n_t <- power.t.test(delta = original_mean, sd = original_sd, power = pw,
                      sig.level = 0.05, type = "one.sample")$n
  tibble(Power = scales::percent(pw), `N (t-test)` = ceiling(n_t),
         `N (Wilcoxon, ~5% more)` = ceiling(n_t / 0.955))
})
knitr::kable(power_rows, caption = sprintf(
  "Sample needed to detect the original effect (%.2f%% rare minus common, d_z = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .05.",
  original_mean, original_dz))
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half`.

### Planned sample


We recruited from Prolific, with the following criterias: Age 18+, fluent in English, reside in the US, have access to desktop or laptop with keyboard and headphone or earphone. We collected the data until N=120 participants passed the exclusion criteria. 
Based on Pilot A (N=3), participants spent 15 to 20 minutes to complete the task, so we compensated participants for 17 minutes of their time. This is further confirmed by Pilot B data (N=6), with participants median time of 17 minutes.


### Materials

We followed the set-up of Experiment 2 in the original paper:
For the tones sequence, we used 6 of 100 ms pure tones in each sequence, each 400 ms apart. Each tone has frequencies of A/B/C = 1000/1500/500 Hz, with the split of 75% common and 25% rare sequence of tones. 
For the gamble amounts, based on authors' Experiment 2 data, we incorporated 40 trials per type with sure loss of −25.
For the soundcheck, we modified this slightly to 2 screens headphone check with replay (instead of 6) and we required participants to get both check right before proceeding with the experiment. This was done for the interest of time and to enhance participants experience.
The live experiment is available at the link above for reference. <https://psych251.github.io/feng2024/lite/> 

### Procedure

For the experiment sequence and trials design, we followed closely the original Experiment 2 set-up, but for interest of time and to enhance participants experience we dropped the PHQ-8 questionnaires at the end of the experiment. Upon opening the experiment page, each participant started with consent form (agree / disagree to participate), followed by welcome page, volume calibration, and sound check. After passing the sound check, participants were directed to the practice round for familiarization and sequence checks, followed by instructions for the main task and the main task of 120 trials. After finishing the main task, participants were directed to another tone sequence checks, followed by demographics page with optional comments, and debrief.

Each trial has the following timing: 3s fixation, 1.3s gamble delay, 1s outcome, and 2s safe outcome. Just as in the original experiment, we swapped the risky option’s side from left to right (or right to left) every 10 trials.

Based on Pilot A data, each participant took around 15 to 20 minutes to finish the whole experiment (from loading the page to debrief). This is further confirmed by Pilot B data.
We refer interested reader to our live experiment page above for reference.


### Pilot Testing: 

#### Pilot A: 
In Pilot A, we ran the experiment with N=3 participants to check every variables are logged correctly. The completion time for each participant was between 15 to 20 minutes.

#### Pilot B: 
In Pilot B, we ran the experiment in Prolific with N=6 participants (who completed the task). 
In terms of dropout, 13 participants started the experiment: 2 turned down by device check, 3 failed sound check, 1 stopped before starting the task, and 6 successfully completed the task.
In terms of comprehension, all 6 participants who successfully completed the experiment passed sound check and sequence check before and after the task.
The median time taken to complete the task was 17 minutes.
No changes were made after Pilot A and B.




### Analysis plan



**Key analysis of interest.** 

We are interested in the difference between the percentage of risky choices chosen by each participant following rare and common tone sequence (% risky choice with rare - % risky choice with common ), we tested this using 2-sided Wilcoxon rank test against 0.




**Exclusions.** 
We excluded participants who failed the headphone (sound) check or didn't complete the study.



### Differences from the original study


| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | Adults recruited on Prolific (18+, fluent in English)| Adults recruited on Prolific  (18+, fluent in English, based in US ) | No. |
| Platform | Gorilla | JsPsych | No. |
| Headphone Check |6 trials played once  (min. 5 correct to pass), | 2 trials with replay allowed (2/2 correct to pass) | Unlikely, participants who didn't use headphone failed the headphone-check despite allowing replay |
|Sample size | 200  | 120 | Unlikely, with N=120 the power is 80% at the original effect (acceptable level)|
| Other tasks | PHQ-8 / GAD Questionnaires Included  | PHQ-8 / GAD Questionnaires Removed | No. |


### Methods addendum (post data collection)


#### Actual sample

From 297 participants who started the experiment, 277 passed the device check, and 142 passed the sound check. 122 of those finished the experiments, but 1 screened-out participant who retook the sound check and 1 timed-out participant are excluded. We analysed results from 120 participants who passed the device check, sound check, and finished the experiments (without timed-out). The average participants age is 40.3 years, with 62 men and 58 women. The median time to complete the experiment is 18.7 minutes (against 17 mins that we compensated based on the pilot result).

#### Deviations from the preregistered plan

(1) 2 participants' data were removed after data collection (1 due to timed-out and 1 due to retake after failing sound check).
(2) We record the choices based on the key-pressed, due to caps-lock bug which affected 5 people and 234 trials in total.
(3) Correction on handling zeros and ties result in Wilcoxon test, which caused minor change in p-value.



## Results

### Data preparation

Data was recorded from the key-pressed (due to caps-lock bug which affected 5 participants and 234 trials in total, refer to deviations section) and the pre-registered exclusion rules were applied (sound check and completing 120 trials). We reported the key-statistics and report and how they were calculated in the confirmatory analysis section.

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Key test: per participant, % risky choices after rare minus after common sequences;
# two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero, as in the original.
if (nrow(pe) >= 2) {
  print(suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(pe$risk_diff, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided", exact = FALSE)))
  effect_summary(pe$risk_diff) |>
    transmute(N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), d_z = round(dz, 2),
              V, p = fmt_p(p)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Key test: rare minus common risky choices, per participant.")
} else {
  message("Key test not run: it needs at least 2 analysed participants; there are ", nrow(pe), ".")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-coding
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Sensitivity check (deviation from the preregistered coding): the key test with choices as
# saved by the Phase 1 experiment, where an uppercase B (caps lock) was saved as a right-hand choice.
if ("chose_risky_recorded" %in% names(trials) && nrow(pe) >= 2) {
  choice_rows <- trials |> filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id)
  caps <- choice_rows |> filter(response %in% c("B", "N"))
  pe_recorded <- choice_rows |>
    mutate(rare = as.logical(rare)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(risk_diff = round(100 * (mean(chose_risky_recorded[rare]) - mean(chose_risky_recorded[!rare])), 8),
              .groups = "drop")
  bind_rows(
    effect_summary(pe$risk_diff) |> mutate(Coding = "Key pressed (b/B = left, n/N = right): primary"),
    effect_summary(pe_recorded$risk_diff) |> mutate(Coding = "As saved by the experiment (uppercase B = right)")
  ) |>
    transmute(Coding, N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), d_z = round(dz, 2),
              V, p = map_chr(p, fmt_p)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
      "Sensitivity check, choice coding: %d choice trials from %d analysed participants were typed in uppercase (%d of them an uppercase B).",
      nrow(caps), n_distinct(caps$participant_id), sum(caps$response == "B")))
}
```

We did two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 0, for the percentage difference of risky choices after rare and common tone. As shown in the table, with N=120, we get +2.55 mean difference (estimate), 1.44 SEM,  95% confidence interval of [−0.31, 5.40], effect size d_z = mean difference / std. dev of difference =  0.16, and p-value = 0.35. 
Compare to the original studies of mean difference +4.03, 95% CI of [1.94, 6.12], p < .001, and d_z = 0.27.



### Replication assessment


The confidence interval of our replication result includes both 0 and also the original estimate of +4.03, hence we can say our result is inconclusive. 
The calculated effect size d_z = 0.16 is only 60% of the original effect size d_z = 0.27.

### Exploratory analyses

We analysed replay users vs non-replay users after collecting our data and stay rate: rate of people making the same choice as on the previous trial. We also analysed the first half and second half of the trials separately (each with 60 trials: 15 rare tone trials and 45 common tone trials).
The results are reported in the table below. 

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-replay
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory (not preregistered): the rare-tone effect for participants who did and did not use
# Replay in the 2-screen headphone check. Within each group: two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test
# against zero; between groups: two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) test.
replay_use <- trials |>
  filter(task == "headphone_check", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(used_replay = sum(as.numeric(replays), na.rm = TRUE) > 0, .groups = "drop")
pe_replay <- pe |> left_join(replay_use, by = "participant_id")
by_replay <- pe_replay |>
  group_by(Group = if_else(used_replay %in% TRUE, "Used Replay", "No Replay")) |>
  group_modify(~ effect_summary(.x$risk_diff)) |>
  ungroup()
by_replay |>
  transmute(Group, N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), p = map_chr(p, fmt_p)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: rare minus common risky choices by Replay use in the headphone check (Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero within each group).")
rs <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(risk_diff ~ used_replay, data = pe_replay, exact = FALSE))
message(sprintf("Between groups (Wilcoxon rank-sum): W = %.1f, p = %s", rs$statistic, fmt_p(rs$p.value)))
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-halves
```

## Discussion


### Summary of replication attempt
We did two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 0, for the percentage difference of risky choices after rare and common tone (for each person). With N=120, we get +2.55 mean difference (estimate), 1.44 SEM,  95% confidence interval of [−0.31, 5.40], effect size d_z = 0.16, and p-value = 0.35. 
The confidence interval of our replication result includes both 0 and also the original estimate of +4.03, hence we can say our result is inconclusive. The calculated effect size d_z = 0.16 is only 60% of the original effect size d_z = 0.27. 
Our conclusion still holds after robustness check.


### Commentary


The exploratory analysis suggest that the participants who use replay (41 participants) have mean of +1.49 with SEM 2.40, while participants who don't use replay (79 participants) have mean of +3.09 with SEM 1.81. This may suggest that participants who need to use replay button show much smaller effect to risky decision making after rare tone. This exploratory analysis result may have suggested the need for stricter sound check, i.e. dropping replay and restoring the 6 sequences sound checks. 
Furthermore, halving the experiment length, i.e. with 60 trials instead of 120 trials per participant, can potentially reduce experiment fatigue, but has some trade-off involved, as discussed in Phase 2 Extension's Rationale section.


# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:**  Best-practices rescue

## Rationale


There are 3 possible reasons for Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result. First, we had too few sample for a smaller true effect. The effect estimated by our replication is +2.55 and this gives much lower than 80 % power with N=120. We can potentially address this issue by increasing sample size to N=250. 
Second, we had weaker sound check compare to the original paper. With 2 screens sound-check and replay option, guessers pass our 2-screen check around 11% of the time (compare to around 2% in the original paper). Another interesting observation from exploratory analysis suggest that participants who need to use replay button show no effect to risky decision making after rare tone (no replay users   +3.09 ± 1.81 (n=79) and replay users: 1.49 ± 2.40  (n = 41)). We can potentially address this issue by restoring the original 6 screens sound check (pass with 5 out of 6 correct) and removing the replay option.
The third reason is experiment fatigue, based on few participants feedback in the pilot and main study, the 17 minutes duration of the experiment might be too long. One of the possible changes to make is to cut the experiment duration to 10 minutes (i.e. with 60 trials instead of 120 trials per participant). One of the drawback to this change is we would get less chance to observe the risky sound effect for each participants (15 trials instead of 30 trials). However, we can recruit more participants for the similar budget (N=250 to get 80% power for +3 points target effect), and attrition rate would have been reduced. Also, based on the exploratory analysis, the replication result does not provide strong support that effect built up over the session (+2.41 in trials 1–60 vs +2.69 in trials 61–120).


## Changes from Phase 1



| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Checks | 2-screen sound check with Replay, 2/2 to pass |  6-screen sound check, played once, 5/6 to pass | Participants from phase 1 who used replay show no effect, stricter sound check to screened out 'guesser' |
| 2 | Sample | N=120 | N=250 | The effect estimated by our replication is +2.55 and this gives much lower than 80 % power with N=120, also to account for halving the number of trials|
| 3 | Number of trials | 120 trials | 60 trials | Reduce experiment fatigue, reduce participants attrition rate |
| 4 | Case sensitivity (Caps-lock) | saving upper B as right hand side choice | case insensitive: B read as b, N as n | Caps-lock enabled choices in Phase 1 were misrecorded (affected 5 people and 234 trials) and decoding had to be done to sync the data with the actual key pressed |


Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.



## Power and sample



Considering the possible improvement through stricter sound check and no replay and based on the exploratory analysis of replay vs no-replay participants, we would expect the effect to move closer to original 4.03. Balancing the trade-off between effect size and budget constraints, we would power to 3 points instead of the phase 1 result of 2.55 or the original result of 4.03. To achieve at least 80% power at this effect size and half of the trials (60 trials), we would require N=250 participants. Considering the Phase 1 attrition rate and stricter sound-check, we may need 615-770 to start, however we would expect the dropout rate to be reduced with shorter experiment duration.
Full analysis is presented in the table and the power curve below. 




```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n <- 250   # planned analysed participants in Phase 2

# Power of the planned test (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, alpha = .05) by simulation: draw
# samples of n people from individual effects, moved so that the effect equals the target, and
# count how often the test is significant. Phase 2 has 60 choice trials (15 rare), so its
# individual effects are simulated from the Phase 1 effects computed on trials 1-60 only (same
# number of rare and common trials); the Phase 1 row uses all 120 trials. Moving the
# effects to the target: the effects are shifted so that their PSEUDO-MEDIAN (Hodges-Lehmann
# estimate, what the Wilcoxon test is about) equals the target, i.e. every person's effect moves
# by the same amount ("effect in everyone"). If instead only a few people carried the effect, as
# in Phase 1 (median 0), power would be much lower: power_at(..., centre = "mean") gives that case.
# Falls back to a one-sample t approximation with the original SD if there are no Phase 1 data.
# The CI half-width (for the mean) uses the SD of the same individual effects.
first_60 <- function(d) {
  d$trials <- d$trials |> filter(!(task %in% "choice") | as.numeric(trial_number) <= 60)
  d
}
basis <- if (have_data) list(`Phase 1 (actual)`  = person_effects(phase1)$risk_diff,
                             `Phase 2 (planned)` = person_effects(first_60(phase1))$risk_diff)
p1_effect <- if (have_data) effect_summary(basis$`Phase 1 (actual)`)
n_sim     <- 2000
hodges_lehmann <- function(x) { w <- outer(x, x, "+") / 2; median(w[upper.tri(w, diag = TRUE)]) }

power_at <- function(study, n, delta, centre) {
  if (is.null(basis)) {
    return(power.t.test(n = n, delta = delta, sd = original_sd, sig.level = 0.05, type = "one.sample")$power)
  }
  x0 <- basis[[study]]
  shifted <- x0 - (if (centre == "mean") mean(x0) else hodges_lehmann(x0)) + delta
  mean(replicate(n_sim, {
    x <- round(sample(shifted, n, replace = TRUE), 8)
    suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(x, mu = 0, exact = FALSE)$p.value) < 0.05
  }))
}
half_width <- function(study, n) {
  s <- if (is.null(basis)) original_sd else sd(basis[[study]])
  qt(0.975, n - 1) * s / sqrt(n)
}
p1_est <- if (!is.null(p1_effect)) p1_effect$estimate else NA_real_
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)

set.seed(251)
expand_grid(
  Study  = c(if (!is.null(p1_effect)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  centre = if (is.null(basis)) "mean" else "pseudo-median"
) |>
  mutate(Trials       = if_else(Study == "Phase 2 (planned)", 60, 120),
         `N analysed` = if_else(Study == "Phase 2 (planned)", as.numeric(phase2_n), if (!is.null(p1_effect)) as.numeric(p1_effect$N) else NA_real_),
         Assumption   = if (is.null(basis)) "Normal (t approximation)"
                        else "Effect in everyone",
         `Power at 4.03 (original)`  = pct(pmap_dbl(list(Study, `N analysed`, centre), \(s, n, cen) power_at(s, n, original_mean, cen))),
         `Power at 3`                = pct(pmap_dbl(list(Study, `N analysed`, centre), \(s, n, cen) power_at(s, n, 3, cen))),
         `Power at Phase 1 estimate` = if (is.na(p1_est)) "" else pct(pmap_dbl(list(Study, `N analysed`, centre), \(s, n, cen) power_at(s, n, p1_est, cen))),
         `95% CI half-width`         = sprintf("±%.2f points", map2_dbl(Study, `N analysed`, half_width))) |>
  select(Study, Trials, Assumption, `N analysed`, starts_with("Power"), `95% CI half-width`) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
    "Power of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-sided, alpha = .05), %s, and expected precision of the mean%s.",
    if (is.null(basis)) "one-sample t approximation with the original SD" else sprintf("by simulation (%d resamples of Phase 1 individual effects, each shifted so the typical person's effect equals the target, i.e. the effect is in everyone; Phase 2 uses the effects from Phase 1 trials 1-60)", n_sim),
    if (is.na(p1_est)) "" else sprintf("; Phase 1 estimate = %.2f points", p1_est)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-phase2-power-curve
#| fig-cap: "Power of the Phase 2 key test (Wilcoxon signed-rank, two-sided, alpha = .05) by number of analysed participants, for three effect sizes, simulated from the Phase 1 individual effects on trials 1-60 (Phase 2 has 60 trials), assuming the effect is in everyone. Dashed line: 80% power; dotted line: the planned sample."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# Same simulation as the power table above, over a grid of sample sizes (fewer resamples per
# point to keep the render quick). With 60 trials each person's score moves in steps of about
# 2.2 points, so nearby effect sizes (e.g. the Phase 1 estimate and 3) can give similar power.
n_sim_table <- n_sim
n_sim <- 500
set.seed(252)
curve_effects <- c(if (!is.na(p1_est)) p1_est, 3, original_mean)
curve_labels  <- c(if (!is.na(p1_est)) sprintf("Phase 1 estimate (%.2f)", p1_est), "Planning target (3)",
                   sprintf("Original (%.2f)", original_mean))
power_curve <- expand_grid(n = seq(50, 400, by = 25), i = seq_along(curve_effects)) |>
  mutate(Effect = factor(curve_labels[i], levels = curve_labels),
         power  = map2_dbl(n, i, \(n, i) power_at("Phase 2 (planned)", n, curve_effects[i], "pseudo-median")))
n_sim <- n_sim_table
ggplot(power_curve, aes(n, power, colour = Effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = phase2_n, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey25") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c("#B8792A", "#1E6E76", "grey45")[seq_along(curve_labels)], curve_labels)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Analysed participants (Phase 2, 60 trials)", y = "Power", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-recruitment
#| eval: !expr have_data
# How many people need to START Phase 2 to end with phase2_n analysed, using the Phase 1
# attrition at each step (device check, headphone check, finishing, exclusions). The stricter
# 6-screen headphone check is expected to screen out more people, so the headphone pass rate is
# also shown at 90% and 80% of its Phase 1 value. Rows of participants.csv are sessions.
p1p <- phase1$participants
rates <- c(device    = mean(p1p$device_supported %in% TRUE),
           headphone = sum(p1p$headphone_passed %in% TRUE) / sum(p1p$device_supported %in% TRUE),
           finish    = nrow(phase1$complete |> filter(headphone_passed %in% TRUE)) / sum(p1p$headphone_passed %in% TRUE),
           analysed  = nrow(phase1$keep) / nrow(phase1$complete |> filter(headphone_passed %in% TRUE)))
tibble(`Headphone pass rate` = c("As in Phase 1", "90% of Phase 1", "80% of Phase 1"),
       hp = rates[["headphone"]] * c(1, 0.9, 0.8)) |>
  mutate(overall = rates[["device"]] * hp * rates[["finish"]] * rates[["analysed"]],
         `Starters needed` = ceiling(phase2_n / overall),
         `Screened out by headphone check (approx.)` = round(`Starters needed` * rates[["device"]] * (1 - hp))) |>
  transmute(`Headphone pass rate`, `Pass rate` = scales::percent(hp, accuracy = 1),
            `Analysed per starter` = scales::percent(overall, accuracy = 1),
            `Starters needed`, `Screened out by headphone check (approx.)`) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
    "Recruitment needed for %d analysed Phase 2 participants, from Phase 1 attrition: device check passed %s, headphone check passed %s of those, finished %s of those, analysed %s of those.",
    phase2_n, scales::percent(rates[["device"]], 1), scales::percent(rates[["headphone"]], 1),
    scales::percent(rates[["finish"]], 1), scales::percent(rates[["analysed"]], 1)))
```

## Analysis plan


For Phase 2 analysis, we will perform the same test as in Phase 1: Wilcoxon two-sided signed rank test on percentage difference of risky choice after rare and common tone for each participant. Participants data will only included to the analysis for Phase 2 if they obtained  5 out of 6 correct on sound-check and completed all 60 trials. 
For exploratory analysis, we will report the pooled estimates across Phase 1 and Phase 2. We will also report the pooled estimate of participants in Phase 1 who did not use replay and Phase 2 participants, as this is a closer comparison to Phase 2 compare to considering every Phase 1 participants.

We will run Phase 2 under a new experiment id to avoid mixing the result with Phase 1.

**Bot Extension**

As an exploratory extension to this project, we would like to train cognitive science based models to closely match human performance and choices in the risky sound and decision making task; we aim to learn which model can closely replicate human performance.


```{r}
#| label: phase2-pooled
#| eval: !expr have_phase2 && have_data
# Exploratory (as planned in the Phase 2 analysis plan): pooled estimates of the key effect,
# (1) all Phase 1 and Phase 2 participants, and (2) Phase 1 participants who did not use Replay
# in the headphone check together with the Phase 2 participants. Same test as the key analysis.
# Note: Phase 1 effects come from 120 trials (30 rare) and Phase 2 effects from 60 (15 rare),
# so Phase 2 individual effects are noisier; the pooled estimate weights every person equally.
p1_pe <- person_effects(phase1)
p2_pe <- person_effects(phase2)
p1_no_replay <- phase1$trials |>
  filter(task == "headphone_check", participant_id %in% phase1$keep$participant_id) |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(used_replay = sum(as.numeric(replays), na.rm = TRUE) > 0, .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!used_replay) |>
  pull(participant_id)
bind_rows(
  effect_summary(c(p1_pe$risk_diff, p2_pe$risk_diff)) |> mutate(Sample = "Phase 1 + Phase 2"),
  effect_summary(c(p1_pe$risk_diff[p1_pe$participant_id %in% p1_no_replay], p2_pe$risk_diff)) |>
    mutate(Sample = "Phase 1 without Replay users + Phase 2")
) |>
  transmute(Sample, N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), d_z = round(dz, 2), p = map_chr(p, fmt_p)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: pooled rare minus common risky choices (Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero).")
```

Compare Phase 2 with Phase 1 and with the original, using the Key statistics table and the figure

reasons recover the effect? For a scientific extension, what does the new condition show? End

# Data and code availability

The experiment code, the anonymized data, and the code that produces every number in this
report are available at <https://github.com/psych251/feng2024>. The experiment itself can be
taken at <https://psych251.github.io/feng2024/phase2>. The data contain no names, email addresses,
IP addresses, or Prolific IDs; the file linking participants to their Prolific IDs is kept
privately for payment and is not shared.
